column1: # Shared block-dangerous cases, read by BOTH test-hooks.ps1 and test-hooks.sh.
# Why a table and not twin hand-written cases: two suites holding the same
# string do not test the same thing, they only look like they do. A case here
# is executed once per dialect against the dialect's own hook, so the two
# implementations are compared rather than the two test files.
# Format, tab-separated, four fields:
#   name <TAB> branch <TAB> expect <TAB> json
# Lines starting with '#' and blank lines are ignored. The json field is last
# because it is the only one that may contain spaces; it may not contain tabs.
# What may live here: only cases whose command is dialect-neutral and whose
# verdict means the same thing in both harnesses. PowerShell resolves the
# hook's output by parsing it; bash matches on substrings. Measured, they agree
# on 'deny', 'allow' and 'ask' for any syntactically valid single JSON
# statement, and on 'silent' whenever the hook emits exactly '{}'. They do NOT
# agree when it emits nothing at all: PowerShell reads empty or whitespace
# output as 'silent' while bash has no match for it, and a non-zero exit is
# 'error' in PowerShell against a separate fault path in bash. So a 'silent'
# case belongs here only once the hook's '{}' output has been measured on both
# sides, and 'notdeny' stays inline until that difference is closed.
# PowerShell-only syntax (Remove-Item, the call operator, `powershell
# -Command`) stays inline because it is not a shared command at all.
# The twin-coverage ratchet in test-hooks.sh counts these rows for both
# dialects. Adding a row here closes the gap by one; deleting one reopens it.
# name
git status is safe
git diff is safe
git add specific file is safe
git commit is safe
git merge auto-allowed at balanced default
git config read is safe
